name: Gladstone
title: Thickness Measurement at Gladstone | Coal, LNG & Bauxite Ships
description: Gladstone ship thickness measurement for coal, bauxite and LNG carriers: holds, hoppers, ballast tanks and hull plating gauged at anchor or alongside.
h1: Ultrasonic Gauging for Bulk and LNG Carriers at Gladstone
intro: Gladstone, on Port Curtis in central Queensland, is the state's largest multi-commodity port: coal leaves through two big export terminals, LNG through three plants on Curtis Island, and bauxite, alumina, aluminium and cement move through the wharves serving the town's refineries and smelter. That brings Capesize and Panamax bulk carriers, LNG carriers and bauxite ships to a harbour with no shipyard, so gauging is done alongside or at anchor. Technicians travel from India to each ship; Atlantis has nobody stationed in Australia.

highlights.h: Coal ships at RG Tanna and WICET
highlights.p: Bulk carriers loading at the RG Tanna Coal Terminal and the Wiggins Island Coal Export Terminal face the hold and hopper wastage typical of the coal trade. Gauging is timed to the clean-hold inspection and the loading sequence, or done at anchor while the ship waits for its slot.

Bauxite arrives by sea for the two alumina refineries, discharged at South Trees and Fisherman's Landing, often in ships that return to Gladstone again and again. Repeat calls let an owner spread condition gauging and hold inspections across several voyages instead of waiting for the next docking.

LNG carriers load at three separate plant wharves on Curtis Island. The cargo containment system is outside a gauging scope, but ballast tanks, hull structure, deck piping and machinery-space pipework can be measured where the terminal operator and the ship's manager agree to it.

port.h: Port Curtis, Curtis Island and the approach from the reef coast
p: Gladstone's harbour is Port Curtis, a deep, natural harbour sheltered by Curtis and Facing islands, about 525 kilometres north of Brisbane near the southern end of the Great Barrier Reef. Ships approach from the open sea through a long dredged channel into the harbour, then follow the inner channels to the wharf centres on the mainland or to the LNG wharves on Curtis Island. Gladstone Ports Corporation, owned by the Queensland government, manages the port and carries out its pilotage, which is compulsory for merchant ships, while Maritime Safety Queensland's regional harbour master sets the navigation rules. Ships waiting for a berth or a cargo anchor in designated areas outside the harbour. Bulk carriers often queue for coal berths, and the agent's line-up of expected arrivals is the starting point for planning any visit.

The harbour serves an industrial complex rather than a city. Coal from central Queensland's Bowen and Callide basins is loaded at the RG Tanna Coal Terminal, the port's largest wharf centre, and at the industry-owned Wiggins Island Coal Export Terminal. On Curtis Island, the Queensland Curtis LNG, Santos GLNG and Australia Pacific LNG projects each run their own plant and wharf, shipping liquefied coal seam gas mainly to North Asia. Bauxite is imported for the Queensland Alumina refinery's wharf at South Trees and for Fisherman's Landing, which also handles alumina, caustic soda, ammonia, acid and cement products; the Boyne smelter's wharf ships aluminium. Auckland Point takes petroleum products, LPG, grain, containers and the occasional cruise ship, and Barney Point now handles calcite and woodchip.

The weather is tropical. From roughly November to April, cyclones in the Coral Sea can force ships out of the anchorage and close the port, and heavy rain and thunderstorms interrupt deck work; the cooler, drier months suit open-deck gauging best. The tidal range in Port Curtis is large by east-coast standards, and strong tidal streams run in the harbour channels, which affects boat transfers and berthing times. Because the port sits within the Great Barrier Reef World Heritage Area, shipping movements, ballast water and any discharge are watched closely, and ships waiting at anchor keep to their designated areas. Summer heat also matters below deck, where tank temperatures limit how long a technician can safely work inside a confined space before a break.

facilities.h: Where ships at Gladstone can be gauged
p: Gladstone work is done alongside or at anchor. At the coal terminals, hold gauging fits into the window between the clean-hold inspection and the start of loading, and ballast, topside and hopper tanks follow the deballasting sequence; at the bauxite, alumina and cement wharves, discharge and loading decide access. At the Curtis Island LNG wharves each plant operator runs its own terminal rules, and a visiting team's access has to be agreed well in advance through the agent and the ship's manager. Ships at the anchorage can be boarded by boat in suitable weather, which is the most useful option for empty-hold work on a waiting bulk carrier.

The port has no drydock or shipyard for ocean-going ships. Bulk carriers and LNG carriers trading here dock in Asia, so Gladstone readings feed a pre-docking steel estimate or an owner's condition record rather than steel renewal on the spot. Tugs, pilot vessels, workboats and the ferries serving the harbour islands are maintained locally on slipways and hardstands, and these smaller craft can be gauged when they are out of the water.
list: RG Tanna Coal Terminal — Capesize and Panamax holds, hoppers and topside tanks, timed to the loading sequence.
Wiggins Island Coal Export Terminal — the same bulk carrier gauging, coordinated with the terminal's berth plan.
Curtis Island LNG wharves — ballast tanks, hull structure and deck piping on LNG carriers, within each operator's rules.
South Trees and Fisherman's Landing — bauxite, alumina and cement ships; hold and tank gauging during discharge or loading.
Auckland Point — product tankers, LPG carriers and general cargo ships; tanks, deck and piping.
Anchorage outside the harbour — empty-hold, ballast tank and pre-purchase gauging on waiting ships, boarded by boat.
Local slipways — tugs, pilot vessels, workboats and island ferries.

context.h: AMSA, Queensland and shipping inside the reef
p: AMSA carries out port state control at Gladstone, as at every Australian port, under Australia's membership of the Tokyo MoU and the Indian Ocean MoU; bulk carriers dominate the inspections here and their structure is a routine part of them. Maritime Safety Queensland oversees navigation in the state's ports, and together with AMSA it runs REEFVTS, the vessel traffic service covering the Great Barrier Reef and Torres Strait, which follows ships moving along the reef coast to and from Gladstone. A structural failure or loss of power near the reef has consequences well beyond the ship itself, which is a strong reason to keep hull and tank condition records current for ships in this trade.

Biosecurity and the environment shape port calls here. International arrivals report their biofouling management to the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry before entering Australian seas, and ballast water must be managed to Australian rules, a sensitive matter in a harbour bordered by seagrass and reef. LNG carriers are vetted by the plant operators and their buyers, while the coal and bauxite ships are screened by charterers and miners, often using RightShip ratings; recent thickness readings and steel renewal records help an older ship through both kinds of vetting.

jobs.h: Typical gauging work for ships at Gladstone
jobs.p: Gladstone enquiries come mostly from bulk carrier owners and managers. Coal ships need hold frame, hopper and topside tank readings before surveys, sales and charter renewals; bauxite and alumina ships on regular runs suit condition monitoring visits spread across their repeat calls; LNG carrier operators ask for ballast tank and hull structure readings between dockings. With no yard in the port, the work is owner's condition gauging, pre-purchase inspection or a steel estimate for a docking in Asia. We agree the scope with the superintendent around the loading slot or anchorage period, mobilise the team from India when the visa and the ship's arrival are settled, and report on the class formats so the readings carry forward into the next survey.
list: Hold and hopper gauging on a Capesize bulk carrier waiting off Gladstone for a slot at RG Tanna, ahead of its renewal survey.
Condition monitoring on a bauxite carrier, with a different group of holds and tanks measured on each Gladstone call.
Ballast tank and hull structure gauging on an LNG carrier between dockings, arranged with the Curtis Island operator.
Pre-purchase inspection of a Panamax bulk carrier at anchor, covering holds, hatch covers and ballast tanks.
Hull gauging of a harbour tug or island ferry on a local slipway.

logistics: Gladstone Airport has domestic flights, mostly from Brisbane, and Rockhampton to the north-west is an alternative with more connections; international arrivals come through Brisbane. Indian nationals need an Australian visa for short-term specialist work, applied for when the ship's arrival window is known, as processing times vary. Terminal access, escorts within port security zones and boats to the anchorage are arranged through the ship's agent, and access to Curtis Island goes through the LNG plant operator.
vessels: Tugs, pilot vessels and island ferries

faqs.q: Is there anywhere to dock a ship at Gladstone?
faqs.a: Not an ocean-going ship. The port has no drydock or shipyard for bulk carriers or LNG carriers, which dock in Asia. Gladstone's role is to provide the readings beforehand: holds, tanks and hatch covers gauged at anchor or alongside, so the yard receives a measured steel estimate. Only harbour craft such as tugs, pilot vessels and ferries are maintained on local slipways.

faqs.q: Can the team board an LNG carrier at a Curtis Island wharf?
faqs.a: Possibly, but it needs early planning. Each LNG plant has its own access and safety rules, loading is a tightly controlled operation, and the operator has to agree to a visiting team. Ballast tanks, hull structure and deck piping are the realistic scope during a loading call. Where the operator prefers, the same work can be done while the ship waits at anchor.

faqs.q: Does the cyclone season stop work at Gladstone?
faqs.a: It can interrupt it. Between roughly November and April a cyclone in the Coral Sea can close the port and send ships from the anchorage to sea, and storms halt open-deck work. Tank gauging carries on once the team is aboard and the ship is safely alongside. Where the owner has a choice, we plan deck-heavy scopes and anchorage work for the drier months.

faqs.q: Can gauging be spread across a bauxite ship's repeat calls?
faqs.a: Yes. Ships on a regular bauxite run come back to Gladstone often, so an owner can set a programme of holds, ballast tanks and hatch covers to measure on successive calls, building a full condition record without delaying the ship. The measurement points are fixed and marked, so readings can be trended from one visit to the next.
